newsitem.title: USA: Miami commuter tax doomed by state constitution.
newsitem.headline: Miami commuter tax doomed by state constitution.

text.p: Miami's attempt to levy a commuter tax on workers who live outside of the city appears doomed due to legal conflicts, Assistant City Manager Bill Hampton said Friday.

City Attorney A. Quinn Jones has advised that the tax would probably violate Florida's constitutional prohibition against income taxes. Such a tax could only be authorized if voters approve a constitutional amendment, he said.
"It doesn't seem like a viable approach," Hampton said. "In our state, in our lifetime, we'll never see the people vote for a change in the constitution to permit that."
Miami Mayor Joe Carollo had proposed a $10 monthly tax on the 600,000 people who work in Miami but live outside the city limits. The tax would have raised up to $72 million a year.
The city is scraping for new revenues to help close a $68 million gap in its $275 million budget for the year that began October 1.

Instead of the commuter tax, the city is now considering a fire-rescue district tax on all property owners. That would remove the $52 million fire-rescue budget from the city's general fund, enabling it to use ad valorem taxes for other purposes, Hampton said.
The proposal would apply to all property owers within the city limites, including churches, schools and government buildings that are exempt from ad valorem taxes.
"What they're saying is, this fire service is provided for eveybody in the use district and why should one portion of the district pay for the others who are not paying," Hampton said.
However, he said the plan is expected to be controversial, especially among poor church congregations who could not afford to pay.
"That'll all have to be addressed," Hampton said."
Municipal rating analysts from Standard & Poor's Corp also met with city officials Friday, but none who attended the meeting were available for comment.

S&P put the city's single-A bond rating on CreditWatch with negative implications, citing the budget deficit. Moody's Investors Service cut its rating for Miami's general obligtion debt to Baa from single-A last week.
